references.text: The preceding verse provides the context: the older son came home from the field and approached the house, which led him to call one of the servants to ask what was happening ([ref:Luk 15:25|Luke 15:25]).

The servant answers the question asked in verse 26 and explains that his brother has come home, and that the father has killed the fattened calf because he has received him back safe and sound ([ref:Luk 15:27|Luke 15:27]).
The parable of the lost sheep contains the same theme of joy and celebration at reunion, which is the background for the feast the older son asks about ([ref:Luk 15:6-7|Luke 15:6-7]).
The parable of the lost coin has the same motif of joy over what was found, parallel to the feast that took place when the younger son came home ([ref:Luk 15:9-10|Luke 15:9-10]).

When Joseph's brothers sent his bloodied robe to Jacob, they asked what this was – a motif of a family member seeking information about another family member's fate, parallel to the older son asking the servant ([ref:1 Mos 37:32-33|Genesis 37:32-33]).

A man from Benjamin came running from the battlefield, and Eli asked what had happened – a similar pattern where someone asks about the cause of the commotion or event ([ref:1 Sam 4:16|1 Samuel 4:16]).

The disciples asked Jesus what the parable meant – a parallel question about the meaning behind something they did not understand, like the older son's question to the servant ([ref:Luk 8:9|Luke 8:9]).
